top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was conducted only for outcomes reported by at least three non-overlapping primary studies with extractable numerators and denominators. Pooled incidences were estimated using random-effects models for proportions, with variance stabilization for rare events where appropriate. Results were expressed as pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran Q and the I-squared statistic. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. We prespecified subgroup exploration by age group, ERCP indication, procedure type, pancreatic duct manipulation or contrast injection, sphincterotomy, and operator or center volume. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. ARTICLE IN PRESS Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger test only for outcomes with at least ten eligible studies. Funnel plots were not generated for rare outcomes with fewer than ten studies because asymmetry tests would be unreliable. All tests were two-sided. For analyses other than Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For Cochran's Q test, P < 0.10 was considered indicative of potential between-study heterogeneity because this test has limited power when relatively few studies are included. Heterogeneity was interpreted together with I² and τ². AI-assisted tools were used during revision for language editing and formatting checks. The authors verified the data extraction, statistical analyses, interpretation, and final text and take full responsibility for the manuscript.

top_evidence.text: This systematic review included 65 sources in the qualitative synthesis, consisting primarily of contemporary pediatric ERCP primary studies and selected prior systematic reviews or meta-analyses used for contextual benchmarking[2-14, 19-71]. Prior reviews were not treated as independent primary data and their pooled estimates were not combined with overlapping primary studies. A detailed account of the literature screening and selection process, following PRISMA 2020 principles, is illustrated in Figure 1.

top_evidence.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020[15]. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251084264), in accordance with best practice guidelines to ensure transparent reporting and reduce reporting bias.

top_evidence.text: The methodological quality and risk of bias of each eligible source were independently assessed by two reviewers using tools appropriate to study design. Disagreements were resolved by consensus, with a third reviewer consulted when needed. Non-randomized primary studies were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), randomized trials using RoB 2, and prior systematic reviews or meta-analyses using AMSTAR 2[16-18]. Rather than reproducing checklist content, we summarized each study's overall judgment and used these judgments to grade confidence across evidence domains. Risk-of-bias judgments informed the narrative synthesis. Studies with incomplete adverse-event definitions, unclear denominators, overlapping cohorts, or high risk of selection or reporting bias were interpreted cautiously and were not used to support quantitative claims beyond their reported data.

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: The available evidence suggested that ERCP indication influenced complication patterns. Children undergoing ERCP for acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis were repeatedly reported to have higher PEP risk than those undergoing ERCP for choledocholithiasis, although the magnitude of association varied by study design, adjustment strategy, and procedural case mix. The overall incidence of post-ERCP complications in children varied across studies because of differences in patient populations, procedural indications, adverse-event definitions, and follow-up. Random-effects pooling was performed for PEP because this outcome had the most consistently extractable numerators and denominators. Figure 2 presents the study-level forest plot for PEP incidence after pediatric ERCP. Bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis were less frequent and were summarized descriptively when study-level event data were sparse or inconsistently reported. PEP : PEP was the most frequent and clinically significant complication associated with pediatric ERCP. In the present synthesis, 15 non-overlapping primary studies contributed extractable PEP event counts, yielding a pooled incidence of 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%) under a random-effects model. Table 1 now reports the study-level numerator, denominator, percentage, denominator unit, and available definition or reporting note for every study contributing to the PEP synthesis. The rows most dependent on percentage backcalculation or source-unit interpretation were rechecked against the original source records for Goetz, Mercier, Perera, and Batibay[24, 60, 63, 72]. ARTICLE IN PRESS The high I-squared value indicates real between-study inconsistency rather than a single uniform pediatric PEP risk. Likely contributors include age distribution, acute recurrent or chronic pancreatitis as the indication, pancreatic duct cannulation or contrast injection, pancreatic sphincterotomy, difficult cannulation, operator and center volume, trainee participation, follow-up windows, and differences in PEP definitions. Denominator unit was another source of variation: some studies reported ERCP procedures, whereas others reported patients or first ERCP per child. Because repeat ERCPs per child were not consistently available, procedure-level data were not converted to patient-level data. In the post hoc denominator-unit summary, procedure-level studies contributed 181 PEP events among 2669 ERCPs (crude rate, 6.8%), patient-level or first-ERCP-per-child studies contributed 20 events among 421 children (4.8%), and the mixed or unclear-denominator study contributed 12 events among 232 observations (5.2%). Heterogeneity persisted after this separation, so the pooled estimate should be interpreted as a contemporary benchmark rather than a single individualized risk estimate. Most pediatric PEP cases are mild and resolve with conservative management, whereas a minority progress to moderate or severe PEP with prolonged hospitalization, systemic inflammatory response, pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst formation, or rarely mortality[4, 59, 73]. The Atlanta classification, originally developed for adults, is often applied in pediatric settings but has not been fully validated for pediatric post-ERCP pathophysiology [62]. Visual inspection of the PEP funnel plot suggested possible small-study effects, although Egger regression did not show clear statistical evidence of asymmetry (intercept, -1.98; approximate two-sided P = 0.16). This result should be interpreted cautiously because heterogeneity was substantial and denominators were reported as either patients or procedures across studies (Figure 8). Bleeding : Post-ERCP bleeding in children most commonly occurs after endoscopic sphincterotomy (EST). Clinically significant bleeding is uncommon, with an estimated incidence of approximately 0.5%[4]. Bleeding may appear during the procedure, shortly afterward, or several days later. Reported risk factors include coagulopathy, larger sphincterotomy incisions, and vascular anomalies. Most cases respond to endoscopic hemostasis with epinephrine injection or clip placement. Severe or endoscopically refractory bleeding may require angiographic embolization; surgery should be reserved for cases in which less invasive measures fail. Perforation : ERCP-related perforation is rare but potentially life-threatening, with an estimated incidence below 1% in pediatric patients[4]. Risk factors include difficult cannulation, excessive force during guidewire or endoscope advancement, anatomical anomalies, and strictures. A practical concern is device size. Pediatric duodenoscopes have become less available in recent years, so clinicians may need to use adult-sized equipment in small children, which can increase mechanical risk. Early recognition matters: minor perforations may be treated conservatively, whereas larger defects often require surgery. Cholangitis : Post-ERCP cholangitis is a recognized infectious complication, typically resulting from incomplete biliary drainage or procedural contamination. Although its incidence in children is less well-defined than that of PEP, it remains clinically important[63]. Risk factors include persistent biliary obstruction, incomplete stone clearance, and prior biliary surgery. Prophylactic antibiotics are commonly considered, particularly in patients with pre-existing cholangitis or immunocompromised status. Management requires prompt antibiotic therapy and restoration of biliary drainage, which may require repeat ERCP or percutaneous intervention. Other complications : Less common complications of ERCP in children include cholecystitis, bile duct injury or stricture, and events related to sedation or anesthesia[13]. Cholecystitis may arise if the cystic duct is obstructed or manipulated during the procedure. Ductal injury is rare but can lead to later stricture formation. Sedation- and anesthesia-related complications are especially relevant in children because of smaller airway size, higher metabolic demand, and age-specific responses to anesthetic agents. Close monitoring by pediatric anesthesia teams is therefore important for procedural safety[64]. The evidence points to a broad but unevenly reported risk profile for pediatric ERCP. Overall complication rates are usually low, but serious events such as PEP, bleeding, perforation, and cholangitis require close attention. Differences in definitions, follow-up, and reporting explain much of the variability across studies. Better pediatric definitions and prospective datasets are needed before risk estimates for rare outcomes can be pooled with confidence. Risk Factors for Complications Operator background also influenced complication rates. Pediatric series and adult operator-volume data[66, 68, 69] suggest that procedures performed by less experienced operators or outside specialized pediatric endoscopy settings may carry higher procedural risk than procedures performed by experienced pediatric gastroenterologists. These findings support specialized training and referral pathways for complex pediatric ERCP. ARTICLE IN PRESS Identifying risk factors for post-ERCP complications in children helps guide patient selection, preprocedural optimization, and intra-procedural risk mitigation. Across the literature, both patient characteristics and procedural variables were associated with adverse events. Table 2 summarizes major patient- and procedure-related factors associated with higher complication rates, particularly PEP, bleeding, and perforation. To complement this summary, Figure 3 summarizes patient-related and procedure-related risk domains reported across the included literature.
